source_refs.note: Topic 21.10 (heading printed 'OCEAN CURENTS') with the Tidbit and Brain Teaser, answered (PDF 179); Fig 21.11 (a world map) is redrawn as a simplified schematic. Answer needs review.

blocks.text: Ocean currents and wind patterns play an important role in regulating Earth's climate and weather. Ocean currents are large-scale movements of seawater, which circulates in two main ways: across the surface and between the deeper layers. Surface currents are mostly caused by wind pushing water across the ocean's top layer. The vertical circulation of water, driven by differences in temperature and salinity, which affect its density, is called thermohaline circulation (21.13 and 21.14).

The rotation of the Earth also shapes ocean movement, creating large circular current systems called gyres. These spin clockwise in the northern hemisphere and anticlockwise in the southern hemisphere. The currents move warm water from the equator towards the poles and bring cold water back, helping to regulate the planet's climate (Fig 21.11).

Wind patterns are created by uneven heating of the Earth's surface: warm air rises and cooler air moves in, forming distinct wind belts such as the trade winds, westerlies and polar easterlies. These winds not only move surface ocean water but also influence the direction and strength of ocean currents. Together, wind patterns and ocean currents distribute heat and energy across the planet, affecting climate zones and weather.

blocks.alt: A simplified ocean diagram divided by a dashed equator. Above the equator, the North Pacific and North Atlantic gyres are drawn as ovals turning clockwise; below it, the South Pacific, Indian and South Atlantic gyres turn anticlockwise. On each oval the side flowing towards the pole is orange (warm current) and the side flowing towards the equator is blue (cold current).
blocks.caption: Ocean gyres in the two hemispheres (original simplified diagram after Fig 21.11).
blocks.long_description: Winds and the Earth's rotation turn each ocean basin's surface water into a huge loop. Each loop carries warm water poleward on one side and returns cold water on the other.

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: The trade winds that helped ancient sailors navigate are caused by Earth's rotation and solar heating. Changes in ocean currents can change global weather patterns, causing floods in one region and droughts in another.
A storm system is observed rotating clockwise in the southern hemisphere. If an identical system were observed in the northern hemisphere, which way would it rotate, and why?
